stories.headline: Update: US-Iran Post-War Talks Open in Switzerland With 'Encouraging Progress,' Lebanon Fighting Persists
stories.summary:
The first round of formal negotiations between the United States and Iran to finalize a post-war deal concluded in Lucerne, Switzerland, with mediators Qatar and Pakistan declaring "encouraging progress" and announcing agreement on a "roadmap towards reaching a final deal within 60 days." Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi cited "major progress" on ending the conflict in Lebanon, while the joint mediator statement said a communication line had been established to manage vessel passage through the Strait of Hormuz and a "de-confliction cell" created between the US, Iran, and Lebanon.

The negotiations follow a memorandum of understanding signed last week that committed both sides to ending fighting "on all fronts," lifting the US blockade, and launching a $300 billion reconstruction plan for Iran. Iran's lead negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf struck a defiant tone, dismissing Trump's threats to resume military action as signs of "desperation." Iran's supreme leader also publicly distanced himself from the deal, saying Trump signed it "out of desperation."

Despite the diplomatic activity, violence in Lebanon has continued. Israeli strikes have killed dozens of Lebanese civilians according to Beirut's health ministry, and Israel reported four of its own soldiers killed by Hezbollah. A new ceasefire was declared Friday but clashes have persisted, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insisting Israeli forces would remain in southern Lebanon indefinitely. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem rejected any Israeli military presence in the south.

The agreement remains contested on multiple fronts. Iran's shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz — announced Saturday though tracking data showed vessels still transiting — and the ongoing Lebanon fighting represent the first tests of the MoU's implementation. The US warned it would restart military action and reimpose the blockade if Iran does not abandon nuclear ambitions, while analysts on both sides are debating which party can more credibly claim victory from the conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Trump-Meloni Feud Escalates as Italy's Prime Minister Fires Back Over Popularity and Base Access
stories.summary:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni publicly rebuked US President Donald Trump on Sunday, telling him to "focus on your own popularity" after Trump questioned her approval ratings and accused her of failing to support American efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The exchange marks a sharp deterioration in what had been one of the closer US-European bilateral relationships since Trump's return to office, with Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani cancelling a planned trip to Washington early next week.

The dispute escalated from a G7 summit earlier in the week, where Trump claimed in a phone interview with Italian broadcaster La7 that Meloni had "begged" him for a photo and that he "felt sorry for her." Meloni called the claim "senseless" and said she was "frankly stunned," adding that "neither I nor Italy ever beg." Trump on Saturday also accused Meloni of causing "a great logistical inconvenience" by barring the US from using Italian air facilities for military operations against Iran.

Meloni has defended Italy's position on base access as governed by standing bilateral agreements that "cannot be violated" while she is prime minister. She acknowledged publicly that being Trump's ally had not helped her domestic approval ratings. The Italian political spectrum largely rallied behind her, with opposition figures as well as coalition members expressing support for her pushback.

The feud reflects broader strains within the Western alliance over Trump's military campaign against Iran, which Italy did not support. The two leaders had previously clashed over Trump's criticism of Pope Leo XIV, which Meloni called "unacceptable." Meloni had been considered the European leader closest to Trump ideologically, having been the only European head of government to attend his inauguration in January 2025.

stories.headline: Ebola Outbreak Worsening in Congo as USAID Cuts Hamper Response
stories.summary:
An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is accelerating, health officials say, with no approved medicine or vaccine available for the current strain. The response has been complicated by the Trump administration's cuts to USAID, which had previously funded significant portions of outbreak detection, containment, and treatment infrastructure in the region.

The DRC has historically been the epicenter of Ebola outbreaks, and international funding and logistics support have been critical to containing previous surges. Health officials are warning that the reduction in US-backed resources is leaving response teams under-resourced at a moment of growing caseloads. The combination of an active outbreak with no approved therapeutic and diminished international support raises the prospect of wider regional spread.

The situation draws renewed attention to the broader consequences of the dismantling of USAID's global health programs, which critics say have left dangerous gaps in epidemic preparedness. Supporters of the cuts argue that foreign aid spending required reform and that recipient nations should build greater domestic capacity. The Ebola outbreak adds to a list of ongoing public health crises — including a prolonged measles outbreak in Utah — where advocates say federal health infrastructure reductions are having tangible effects.

stories.headline: France Puts Half Its Regions on Red Heat Alert as Temperatures Approach 43°C
stories.summary:
Forty-nine of France's 96 administrative regions were placed under red heat alerts Monday as a severe heatwave pushed temperatures toward 43°C (109°F) in Bordeaux and above 40°C across much of western France. An estimated 63 million people are affected in total, with orange alerts covering dozens of additional regions. French authorities closed 845 schools outright and allowed 1,800 others to release students early.

Three elderly residents of the Gironde region, aged between 80 and 95, died over the weekend partly due to the heat, authorities said. Health Minister Stéphanie Rist warned that many citizens would suffer during the week and urged people to monitor vulnerable relatives and neighbors. National rail operator SNCF asked vulnerable passengers to postpone travel, and several Paris metro lines reduced services due to the conditions.

Meteorologists at Météo-France described the event as "widespread, long-lasting and intense," with temperatures not expected to drop until the end of the week. The heatwave extends beyond France: Madrid is forecast to hit 39°C and Rome 37°C, while Belgium has cancelled peak-hour train services Monday and Tuesday. The extreme heat follows an alcohol ban at France's annual Fête de la Musique festival this past weekend, where large outdoor crowds gathered in already dangerous conditions.
